claim: Fibroblasts from chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), bonobos (Pan paniscus) and humans (Homo sapiens) were reprogrammed to their pluripotent state.
source: Fibroblasts from chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), bonobos (Pan paniscus) and humans (Homo sapiens) were reprogrammed to their pluripotent state as previously described (Brennand et al., 2015) and then differentiated into NPCs.
evidence: The manuscript states this was done as previously described with citation to Brennand et al., 2015, indicating reliance on established methods from prior work.

claim: Reprogrammed cells were differentiated into NPCs.
source: Fibroblasts from chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), bonobos (Pan paniscus) and humans (Homo sapiens) were reprogrammed to their pluripotent state as previously described (Brennand et al., 2015) and then differentiated into NPCs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the differentiation process and references prior methodology.

claim: Neural differentiation was initiated by plating neuralized embryoid bodies (EBs) for a week until neural rosettes became apparent.
source: Briefly, we initiated neural differentiation by plating neuralized embryoid bodies (EBs) for a week until neural rosettes became apparent in the dish.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors.

claim: Dissociated rosettes formed a homogeneous population of NPCs that continued to proliferate in the presence of the mitogen FGF2.
source: Dissociated rosettes formed a homogeneous population of NPCs that continued to proliferate in the presence of the mitogen FGF2 and were positive for the pan-neural progenitor marker Nestin (Figure 1A and B) and cortical neural progenitor markers Pax6 and Foxg1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from the experimental procedure and references figures showing the data.

claim: NPCs were positive for the pan-neural progenitor marker Nestin.
source: Dissociated rosettes formed a homogeneous population of NPCs that continued to proliferate in the presence of the mitogen FGF2 and were positive for the pan-neural progenitor marker Nestin (Figure 1A and B) and cortical neural progenitor markers Pax6 and Foxg1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: NPCs were positive for cortical neural progenitor markers Pax6 and Foxg1.
source: Dissociated rosettes formed a homogeneous population of NPCs that continued to proliferate in the presence of the mitogen FGF2 and were positive for the pan-neural progenitor marker Nestin (Figure 1A and B) and cortical neural progenitor markers Pax6 and Foxg1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Single cell RNA sequencing revealed that each species had similar proportions of cortical markers.
source: The results revealed that each species had similar proportions of cortical markers, indicating that within the cortical-fated cells there was no enrichment for any given layer between the species (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from single cell RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Within the cortical-fated cells there was no enrichment for any given layer between the species.
source: The results revealed that each species had similar proportions of cortical markers, indicating that within the cortical-fated cells there was no enrichment for any given layer between the species (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The manuscript interprets single cell RNA sequencing data to conclude no layer-specific enrichment differences.

claim: Chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs clustered closer to each other than to human NPC lines.
source: The expression profiles of NPCs from chimpanzee and bonobo clustered closer to each other than to human NPC lines derived from iPSC or human embryonic stem cell (ES) (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq clustering analysis shown in Figure 1C–E.

claim: The first principal component (33% of the variance) separated human from chimpanzee and bonobo samples.
source: The first principal component (33% of the variance) separated human from chimpanzee and bonobo samples (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports principal component analysis results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Among the 1196 differentially expressed genes, 52 genes were involved in pathways related to cellular migration.
source: We next focused on genes differentially expressed between Homo and Pan NPCs and found that, among the 1196 differentially expressed genes (Supplementary file 1), 52 genes were involved in pathways related to cellular migration (Fisher's exact test, p<1.07e-24) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene ontology analysis results with statistical significance (Fisher's exact test, p<1.07e-24).

claim: Both chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs were confluent by 24 hr in the scratch assay, while a gap remained at 24 hr in the human NPCs.
source: While both chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs were confluent by 24 hr, a gap remained at 24 hr in the human NPCs (Figure 2A, bottom panels).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from scratch assay experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For all three species, migration movement was directed toward the scratch when compared to random migration.
source: For all three species, migration movement was directed toward the scratch when compared to random migration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis comparing actual migration to simulated random migration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: The distribution of migration speed of cells from the three species differed, with human NPCs moving significantly more slowly than either chimpanzee or bonobo NPCs.
source: The distribution of migration speed of cells from the three species differed, with human NPCs moving significantly more slowly than either chimpanzee or bonobo NPCs (mean migration speed: human = 0.46 ± 0.19 μm /min, chimpanzee = 0.70 ± 0.31 μm /min, bonobo = 0.72 ± 0.35 μm /min, Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative migration speed measurements with statistical comparison shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There were no significant differences in the migration speeds between chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs.
source: By contrast, we did not find significant differences in the migration speeds between chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of migration speeds between chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs.

claim: Significantly reduced outgrowth was observed from human neurospheres (331.7 ± 14.24 μm) relative to chimpanzee and bonobo (392.7 ± 18.86 μm for chimpanzees and 404.3 ± 20.98 μm for bonobos).
source: We observed significantly reduced outgrowth from human neurospheres (331.7 ± 14.24 μm, total of 123 neurospheres analyzed) relative to chimpanzee and bonobo (392.7 ± 18.86 μm for chimpanzees and 404.3 ± 20.98 μm for bonobos; total of 135 neurospheres analyzed) (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements from neurosphere outgrowth assay shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Individual NHP NPCs reached higher instantaneous speeds, had higher migration speeds and migrated further than human NPCs.
source: In conclusion, individual NHP NPCs reached higher instantaneous speeds, had higher migration speeds and migrated further than human NPCs.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes multiple migration measurements reported earlier in the text.

claim: Chimpanzee NPCs showed an increase in area coverage and distance traveled from injection site compared to human NPCs in vivo.
source: Once again, chimpanzee NPCs showed an increase in area coverage and distance traveled from injection site.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from in vivo transplantation experiments, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs migrated faster and covered longer distances than human NPCs, independent of culture conditions.
source: In summary, our data show that chimpanzee and bonobo NPCs migrated faster and covered longer distances than human NPCs, independent of culture conditions.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from both in vitro and in vivo migration experiments.

claim: Faster migration represents a cell autonomous feature of NHP NPCs that could influence the differences in brain size and brain organization between species.
source: We conclude that faster migration represents a cell autonomous feature of NHP NPCs that could influence the differences in brain size and brain organization between species.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the migration data to suggest potential evolutionary implications.

claim: The selected duration of in vivo neuronal growth was 19 weeks, which spans most of the period of prenatal development of pyramidal neurons in the human cortex.
source: The selected duration of in vivo neuronal growth was 19 weeks, which, based on human post-mortem studies, spans most of the period of prenatal development of pyramidal neurons in the human cortex, that is from the emergence of the first cells with pyramidal morphology at 17 weeks gestation until birth (Mrzljak et al., 1988).
evidence: The manuscript justifies the experimental timeline by citing human post-mortem studies (Mrzljak et al., 1988).

claim: Pyramidal neurons were identified and traced at each time point of the study.
source: Neurons with pyramidal morphology were identified and traced at each time point of the study.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure for morphological analysis.

claim: Pyramidal neurons were distinguishable by their large soma, neurites emerging from the cell body, and visible dendritic spines.
source: They were distinguishable by their large soma, neurites emerging from the cell body, and visible dendritic spines (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes morphological criteria used to identify pyramidal neurons, with examples shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The variables reflecting dendritic spine number and density (DSN and DSD) in iPSC-derived neurons significantly differed across the time points examined for both species.
source: The variables reflecting dendritic spine number and density (DSN and DSD) in iPSC-derived neurons significantly differed across the time points examined for both species (Figure 4H–K).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of morphometric measurements over time shown in Figure 4H–K.

claim: The slopes that showed significant positive correlation for both human and chimpanzee values were DSD and DSN.
source: The slopes that showed significant positive correlation for both human and chimpanzee values were DSD and DSN, indicating that the number of dendritic spines from transplanted neurons increased over time, implying neuronal maturation for both species.
evidence: The manuscript reports regression analysis results for dendritic spine measurements.

claim: The number of dendritic spines from transplanted neurons increased over time, implying neuronal maturation for both species.
source: The slopes that showed significant positive correlation for both human and chimpanzee values were DSD and DSN, indicating that the number of dendritic spines from transplanted neurons increased over time, implying neuronal maturation for both species.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the positive correlation of dendritic spine measurements over time as evidence of neuronal maturation.

claim: Comparison between human and chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons revealed a significant effect of species for the variables TDL, MSL, DSN and TREE at different time points.
source: Comparison between human and chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons revealed a significant effect of species for the variables TDL, MSL, DSN and TREE at different time points.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons between species for multiple morphometric variables.

claim: At four weeks PST, neurites from human transplanted neurons began elongating and continued growing until the last time point examined (19 weeks).
source: At four weeks PST, neurites from human transplanted neurons began elongating and continued growing until the last time point examined (19 weeks).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns of dendritic growth observed in human neurons.

claim: The length of dendrites in chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons increased at two weeks PST, with little change afterward.
source: In contrast, the length of dendrites in chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons increased at two weeks PST, with little change afterward.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns of dendritic growth observed in chimpanzee neurons.

claim: The difference in total dendritic length between the species was significant at 2, 8 and 19 weeks.
source: The difference between the species was significant at 2, 8 and 19 weeks.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons of total dendritic length between species at specific time points.

claim: MSL was significantly higher in human neurons compared to chimpanzee neurons at 6, 8 and 19 weeks.
source: Similarly, MSL was significantly higher in human neurons compared to chimpanzee neurons at 6, 8 and 19 weeks (Figure 4M).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons of mean segment length shown in Figure 4M.

claim: At 8 and 19 weeks, the DSN increased rapidly in the human iPSC-derived neurons, producing significantly higher numbers of spines compared to the chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons at eight weeks.
source: The DSN displayed little difference between the species for the first six weeks PST but, at 8 and 19 weeks, the DSN increased rapidly in the human iPSC-derived neurons, producing significantly higher numbers of spines compared to the chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons at eight weeks (Figure 4N).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal changes in dendritic spine number with statistical comparison shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Some aspects of dendritic morphology develop at earlier time-points in chimpanzee neurons compared to human neurons (1–2 weeks; TDL, MSL, and DSN).
source: Our results suggest that some aspects of dendritic morphology develop at earlier time-points in chimpanzee neurons compared to human neurons (1–2 weeks; TDL, MSL, and DSN).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the morphometric data to suggest heterochronic differences in development.

claim: Parts of dendrites with different functions may mature at different rates in each species.
source: However, the pattern is not seen in all of the dendritic variables (Figure 4L–N and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 G, H and J), indicating that parts of dendrites with different functions may mature at different rates in each species.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the variability in morphometric patterns across different dendritic features.

claim: Neurons were positive for pan-neuronal markers (Tuj1, Map2AB, Synapsin1).
source: At this stage, neurons were positive for pan-neuronal markers (Tuj1, Map2AB, Synapsin1) (Figure 5B and C) and cortical markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence characterization shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the percentage of cells positive for neuronal markers between human, chimpanzee and bonobo lines at two, four or six weeks of differentiation.
source: We did not observe significant differences in the percentage of cells positive for these markers between human, chimpanzee and bonobo lines at two, four or six weeks of differentiation (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of marker expression with statistical comparison shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chimpanzee and bonobo cultures showed significantly increased firing rates at earlier time points (two weeks after differentiation).
source: While chimpanzee and bonobo cultures showed significantly increased firing rates at earlier time points (two weeks after differentiation), human cultures showed increased firing rates at later time points (six weeks after differentiation, Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports multielectrode array (MEA) measurements shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Human cultures showed increased firing rates at later time points (six weeks after differentiation).
source: While chimpanzee and bonobo cultures showed significantly increased firing rates at earlier time points (two weeks after differentiation), human cultures showed increased firing rates at later time points (six weeks after differentiation, Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports multielectrode array (MEA) measurements shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The functional data corroborated the developmental differences observed in the morphological features between human and chimpanzee transplanted cells.
source: The functional data corroborated the developmental differences observed in the morphological features between human and chimpanzee transplanted cells (Figure 4L–M).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the functional data in relation to morphological findings.

claim: There was a similar time window (about four to five weeks) when human neuronal developmental features exceeded those of NHPs both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Interestingly, there was a similar time window (about four to five weeks) when human neuronal developmental features exceeded those of NHPs both in vitro and in vivo (compare Figure 4L with Figure 5F), indicating the presence of species-specific cell-autonomous features consistent across the two lines of analysis.
evidence: The manuscript compares temporal patterns across different experimental approaches shown in Figure 4L and Figure 5F.

claim: The presence of species-specific cell-autonomous features is consistent across in vitro and in vivo analyses.
source: Interestingly, there was a similar time window (about four to five weeks) when human neuronal developmental features exceeded those of NHPs both in vitro and in vivo (compare Figure 4L with Figure 5F), indicating the presence of species-specific cell-autonomous features consistent across the two lines of analysis.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the consistency of temporal patterns across experimental conditions as evidence for cell-autonomous features.

claim: Differential expression of genes related to cell migration and aberrant in vitro cell migration has been reported in NPCs derived from patients with neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: The observation of differential gene expression, carries implications that extend beyond evolutionary studies, since differential expression of genes related to cell migration and aberrant in vitro cell migration has been reported in NPCs derived from patients with neuropsychiatric disorders (Brennand et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Brennand et al., 2015) reporting migration abnormalities in neuropsychiatric disorders.

claim: NPC migration is a tightly regulated process in primates.
source: Our results support the notion that NPC migration is a tightly regulated process in primates, and changes in features related to this process are correlated with alterations in fetal cortical neurogenesis and, potentially, pathogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the findings in the context of primate neurodevelopment.

claim: Changes in features related to NPC migration are correlated with alterations in fetal cortical neurogenesis and, potentially, pathogenesis.
source: Our results support the notion that NPC migration is a tightly regulated process in primates, and changes in features related to this process are correlated with alterations in fetal cortical neurogenesis and, potentially, pathogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the broader implications of migration differences.

claim: Otani et al. showed that the level of individual cortical progenitor cell clonal output in primates is regulated cell autonomously.
source: Recently, Otani et al. showed that the level of individual cortical progenitor cell clonal output in primates is also regulated cell autonomously, opening the possibility for comparative in vitro studies using human and NHP NPCs (Otani et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Otani et al., 2016) on cell-autonomous regulation of progenitor output.

claim: Pyramidal neurons represent the most common type of neuron in the cortex and form basic units of cortical microcircuitry.
source: Since cortical pyramidal neurons represent the most common type of neuron in the cortex and form basic units of cortical microcircuitry (DeFelipe and Fariñas, 1992), comparative analyses directed specifically at pyramidal neurons can yield insights into the organization of the microcircuitry that is typical of each species.
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge (DeFelipe and Fariñas, 1992) about pyramidal neurons.

claim: Comparative analyses directed specifically at pyramidal neurons can yield insights into the organization of the microcircuitry that is typical of each species.
source: Since cortical pyramidal neurons represent the most common type of neuron in the cortex and form basic units of cortical microcircuitry (DeFelipe and Fariñas, 1992), comparative analyses directed specifically at pyramidal neurons can yield insights into the organization of the microcircuitry that is typical of each species.
evidence: The manuscript provides rationale for focusing on pyramidal neurons based on their functional importance.

claim: Differences observed in the adult phenotype between humans and chimpanzees likely reflect differences in timing and/or rate of cortical development.
source: Differences observed in the adult phenotype between humans and chimpanzees likely reflect differences in timing and/or rate of cortical development.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an interpretation based on heterochrony concepts.

claim: Sequential hypermorphosis, a type of heterochrony characterized by prolongation of all stages of brain development compared to the ancestral state, has been proposed as an evolutionary mechanism underlying cerebral expansion in humans.
source: In the case of human brain evolution, sequential hypermorphosis, a type of heterochrony characterized by prolongation of all stages of brain development compared to the ancestral state (McNamara, 2002; Vrba, 1998; McKinney, 2002), has been proposed as an evolutionary mechanism underlying cerebral expansion in humans.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior theoretical work (McNamara, 2002; Vrba, 1998; McKinney, 2002) on heterochrony in human evolution.

claim: Humans and apes share a pattern of prolonged postnatal growth in brain size that sets them apart from Old World monkeys.
source: Humans and apes share a pattern of prolonged postnatal growth in brain size that sets them apart from Old World monkeys (Leigh, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior comparative work (Leigh, 2004) on primate brain development.

claim: The maturation of pyramidal neurons appears to be protracted in hominids compared to macaques.
source: Similarly, the maturation of pyramidal neurons appears to be protracted in hominids compared to macaques (Cupp and Uemura, 1980; Petanjek et al., 2011; Sedmak et al., 2018) and in humans compared to chimpanzees (Bianchi et al., 2013a; Teffer et al., 2013), possibly accounting for longer and more branched dendrites with higher numbers of dendritic spines in humans (Bianchi et al., 2013b; Petanjek et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies (Cupp and Uemura, 1980; Petanjek et al., 2011; Sedmak et al., 2018) on pyramidal neuron maturation.

claim: The maturation of pyramidal neurons appears to be protracted in humans compared to chimpanzees.
source: Similarly, the maturation of pyramidal neurons appears to be protracted in hominids compared to macaques (Cupp and Uemura, 1980; Petanjek et al., 2011; Sedmak et al., 2018) and in humans compared to chimpanzees (Bianchi et al., 2013a; Teffer et al., 2013), possibly accounting for longer and more branched dendrites with higher numbers of dendritic spines in humans (Bianchi et al., 2013b; Petanjek et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies (Bianchi et al., 2013a; Teffer et al., 2013) comparing human and chimpanzee pyramidal neurons.

claim: Protracted maturation of pyramidal neurons possibly accounts for longer and more branched dendrites with higher numbers of dendritic spines in humans.
source: Similarly, the maturation of pyramidal neurons appears to be protracted in hominids compared to macaques (Cupp and Uemura, 1980; Petanjek et al., 2011; Sedmak et al., 2018) and in humans compared to chimpanzees (Bianchi et al., 2013a; Teffer et al., 2013), possibly accounting for longer and more branched dendrites with higher numbers of dendritic spines in humans (Bianchi et al., 2013b; Petanjek et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior morphological studies (Bianchi et al., 2013b; Petanjek et al., 2008) and proposes a mechanistic link.

claim: There is little evidence that the simple addition or subtraction of genes is sufficient to explain the observed differences between humans and chimpanzees.
source: Because there is little evidence that the simple addition or subtraction of genes is sufficient to explain the observed differences (Hill and Walsh, 2005), changes in the regulation (levels and patterns of expression) of genes shared between humans and chimpanzees have been proposed to play an important role (King and Wilson, 1975; Enard et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Hill and Walsh, 2005) on genetic differences between species.

claim: Changes in the regulation (levels and patterns of expression) of genes shared between humans and chimpanzees have been proposed to play an important role.
source: Because there is little evidence that the simple addition or subtraction of genes is sufficient to explain the observed differences (Hill and Walsh, 2005), changes in the regulation (levels and patterns of expression) of genes shared between humans and chimpanzees have been proposed to play an important role (King and Wilson, 1975; Enard et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites foundational work (King and Wilson, 1975; Enard et al., 2002) on gene regulation in human evolution.

claim: The expression of genes relevant to developmental events such as migration and dendritic maturation in pyramidal neurons can provide important insights into the underlying mechanisms shaping the differences in the organization of neuronal networks observed in humans and other primates.
source: In particular, the expression of genes relevant to developmental events such as migration and dendritic maturation in pyramidal neurons can provide important insights into the underlying mechanisms shaping the differences in the organization of neuronal networks observed in humans and other primates.
evidence: The manuscript proposes the rationale for studying gene expression in developmental processes.

claim: The availability of post-mortem specimens often limits the extent of the hypotheses that can be addressed in studies using post-mortem brains from human and NHPs.
source: Although studies using post-mortem brains from human and NHPs have provided important insights into developmental differences across species, the availability of specimens often limits the extent of the hypotheses that can be addressed.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a limitation of traditional post-mortem studies.

claim: Recent advances in somatic reprogramming technology make comparative studies possible even in the absence of post-mortem specimens.
source: Recent advances in somatic reprogramming technology make comparative studies possible even in the absence of post-mortem specimens (Marchetto et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Marchetto et al., 2013) demonstrating the utility of iPSC technology for comparative studies.

claim: Changes in neural migration and cortical layering may pathologically affect early dendritic organization and microcircuitry formation in humans.
source: While changes in neural migration and cortical layering may pathologically affect early dendritic organization and microcircuitry formation in humans (Pramparo et al., 2015; Reiner et al., 2016; Muraki and Tanigaki, 2015; Brennand et al., 2015), previous research has not examined migration and early development of pyramidal neurons from an evolutionary perspective.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Pramparo et al., 2015; Reiner et al., 2016; Muraki and Tanigaki, 2015; Brennand et al., 2015) on pathological effects of migration abnormalities.

claim: Previous research has not examined migration and early development of pyramidal neurons from an evolutionary perspective.
source: While changes in neural migration and cortical layering may pathologically affect early dendritic organization and microcircuitry formation in humans (Pramparo et al., 2015; Reiner et al., 2016; Muraki and Tanigaki, 2015; Brennand et al., 2015), previous research has not examined migration and early development of pyramidal neurons from an evolutionary perspective.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in the literature to justify the current study.

claim: The neurodevelopmental differences between humans and chimpanzees would become visible during distinct processes of NPC migration and during the initial establishment of the organization of dendritic trees and functional neuronal maturation in the neocortex.
source: We therefore hypothesized that the neurodevelopmental differences between humans and chimpanzees would become visible during distinct processes of NPC migration and during the initial establishment of the organization of dendritic trees and functional neuronal maturation in the neocortex.
evidence: The manuscript states the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Differential migration patterns were found in human NPCs compared to those of chimpanzee and bonobo based on RNA expression profile analysis and live-cell imaging.
source: We found differential migration patterns in human NPCs compared to those of chimpanzee and bonobo based on RNA expression profile analysis and live-cell imaging.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes key findings from RNA-seq and live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Morphological and functional developmental differences were observed between human and chimpanzee neurons, suggesting differences in the timing of neuronal maturation between the two species.
source: Next, we observed morphological and functional developmental differences between human and chimpanzee neurons, suggesting differences in the timing of neuronal maturation between the two species.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes key findings from morphological and functional analyses.

claim: The strategy applied in this work can be utilized for further studies addressing human brain evolution and the mechanisms underlying the cellular and molecular aspects that are unique to the human brain.
source: The strategy applied in this work can be utilized for further studies addressing human brain evolution and the mechanisms underlying the cellular and molecular aspects that are unique to the human brain.
evidence: The manuscript proposes broader applications of the experimental approach.

claim: Human brain evolution has been characterized by several waves of increases in cranial capacity since the split from the last common ancestor of hominins and African apes.
source: Since the split from the last common ancestor of hominins (Homo) and African apes (Gorilla and Pan spp), human brain evolution has been characterized by several waves of increases in cranial capacity (Carlson et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2000) and selective expansion of regions implicated in complex cognition (Semendeferi et al., 2010; Semendeferi and Damasio, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Carlson et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2000) on cranial capacity evolution.

claim: Human brain evolution has been characterized by selective expansion of regions implicated in complex cognition.
source: Since the split from the last common ancestor of hominins (Homo) and African apes (Gorilla and Pan spp), human brain evolution has been characterized by several waves of increases in cranial capacity (Carlson et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2000) and selective expansion of regions implicated in complex cognition (Semendeferi et al., 2010; Semendeferi and Damasio, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Semendeferi et al., 2010; Semendeferi and Damasio, 2000) on regional brain expansion.

claim: The increase in cranial capacity in fossil hominins has been tied to behavioral changes, including the appearance of the first stone tools and their subsequent elaboration, increases in population size, and the spread of hominins into ecologically challenging habitats.
source: The increase in the cranial capacity in fossil hominins has been tied to behavioral changes, including the appearance of the first stone tools and their subsequent elaboration, increases in population size, and the spread of hominins into ecologically challenging habitats (Ambrose, 2001; Stout, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Ambrose, 2001; Stout, 2011) linking brain size to behavioral evolution.

claim: Comparative analyses of cortical organization between extant primate species suggest that the human brain differs from the brain of other hominid species in several important microstructural aspects.
source: While these changes cannot be inferred directly from the fossil specimens, comparative analyses of cortical organization between extant primate species suggest that the human brain indeed differs from the brain of other hominid species in several important microstructural aspects (Semendeferi et al., 2001; Barger et al., 2007; Semendeferi et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior comparative studies (Semendeferi et al., 2001; Barger et al., 2007; Semendeferi et al., 2011) on brain microstructure.

claim: The dendritic morphology of cortical pyramidal neurons differs between humans and the common chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes).
source: One of these is the dendritic morphology of cortical pyramidal neurons, which differs between humans and the common chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) (Bianchi et al., 2013a).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Bianchi et al., 2013a) on dendritic morphology differences.

claim: Dendrites on human neurons are initially shorter and less branched and have fewer dendritic spines compared to the dendrites of chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons.
source: As our results suggest, dendrites on human neurons are initially shorter and less branched and have fewer dendritic spines compared to the dendrites of chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes morphological findings from the transplantation experiments.

claim: At one point in development -- ranging from six weeks for MSL and eight weeks for TDL and DSN -- dendrites on human iPSC-derived neurons enter a rapid growth and surpass the chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons.
source: At one point in development -- ranging from six weeks for MSL and eight weeks for TDL and DSN -- dendrites on human iPSC-derived neurons enter a rapid growth and surpass the chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons (Figure 4L–N), suggesting the possibility of late initiation of dendritic growth in humans.
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal patterns of dendritic growth shown in Figure 4L–N.

claim: The late initiation of dendritic growth in humans is a possibility suggested by the data.
source: At one point in development -- ranging from six weeks for MSL and eight weeks for TDL and DSN -- dendrites on human iPSC-derived neurons enter a rapid growth and surpass the chimpanzee iPSC-derived neurons (Figure 4L–N), suggesting the possibility of late initiation of dendritic growth in humans.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the temporal patterns as suggesting delayed initiation of growth in humans.

claim: The morphological findings are supported by the analysis of neuronal function.
source: The morphological findings are supported by the analysis of neuronal function.
evidence: The manuscript states that functional data corroborate morphological observations.

claim: Human neurons in culture displayed functional developmental delay compared to chimpanzee and bonobo neurons.
source: The human neurons in culture also displayed functional developmental delay compared to chimpanzee and bonobo neurons, with human neurons showing increased firing rates and neuronal bursts at later time points.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes functional maturation data from MEA experiments.

claim: Cell-autonomous characteristics of neuronal maturation in humans are different from those of chimpanzees and bonobos.
source: Our results suggest the presence of cell-autonomous characteristics of neuronal maturation in humans that are different from those of chimpanzees and bonobos and support the idea that developmental delay in humans results in increased neuronal complexity (increased dendritic length, spine density) and neuronal function (increased firing rates and network bursts) at later time points during maturation.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the combined morphological and functional data as evidence for cell-autonomous differences.

claim: Developmental delay in humans results in increased neuronal complexity (increased dendritic length, spine density) and neuronal function (increased firing rates and network bursts) at later time points during maturation.
source: Our results suggest the presence of cell-autonomous characteristics of neuronal maturation in humans that are different from those of chimpanzees and bonobos and support the idea that developmental delay in humans results in increased neuronal complexity (increased dendritic length, spine density) and neuronal function (increased firing rates and network bursts) at later time points during maturation.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic interpretation linking developmental timing to neuronal complexity.

claim: The novel strategy combining iPSC technology with in vitro analysis of cell migration and in vivo grafting offers a paradigm aimed at elucidating the genetic underpinnings of the observed changes.
source: As soft tissue remains scarce in human developmental and evolutionary neuroanatomy studies, the novel strategy we present here - combining the use of iPSC technology with in vitro analysis of cell migration and in vivo grafting - offers a paradigm aimed at elucidating the genetic underpinnings of the observed changes and the evolutionary timing of human emergence and suggests further implications for the evolution of cortical microcircuitry across different primate clades.
evidence: The manuscript proposes the broader significance of the experimental approach.

claim: Early developmental events are important for understanding the neuroanatomical changes observed in neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: In addition to their evolutionary importance for specifying species-specific features, early developmental events are important for understanding the neuroanatomical changes observed in neurodevelopmental disorders, since pathologies in dendritic organization tend to appear during the initial establishment of dendrites in Down syndrome, Rett syndrome, autism spectrum disorder, and Fragile X (Marin-Padilla, 1972; Belichenko et al., 1994; Hutsler and Zhang, 2010; Irwin et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Marin-Padilla, 1972; Belichenko et al., 1994; Hutsler and Zhang, 2010; Irwin et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2016) on dendritic pathology in neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: Pyramidal neurons represent a morphological class of neurons with different functional properties.
source: Although pyramidal neurons represent a morphological class of neurons with different functional properties (Chagnac-Amitai et al., 1990; Connors and Gutnick, 1990; Mainen and Sejnowski, 1996), we have adhered to the morphological definition of pyramidal neurons (DeFelipe and Fariñas, 1992; Nieuwenhuys, 1994; Spruston, 2008), which, combined with the quantification of neuronal morphology as utilized in post-mortem studies, enabled a direct comparison of our findings with previous research (Bianchi et al., 2013a; Petanjek et al., 2008; Mrzljak et al., 1988; Mrzljak et al., 1992).
